purpose: Valganciclovir is used to treat a viral eye infection called CMV retinitis in people with HIV/AIDS that can cause blindness. It is also used to prevent a virus called cytomegalovirus (CMV) in people who have received an organ transplant. CMV is a common virus that can be very dangerous in people with weakened immune systems.
how_it_works: When you swallow valganciclovir, your body quickly converts it into an active medicine called ganciclovir. This active medicine works by blocking the virus from copying itself and spreading in your body. Think of it like jamming the copy machine the virus needs to make more of itself — without that ability, the virus cannot grow and cause more damage.
common_side_effects: Low blood cell counts (which can make you feel tired, increase your risk of infections, or cause easy bruising or bleeding), nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, headache, and feeling shaky or unsteady. Some people also experience fever or trouble sleeping.
warnings: This medication can seriously lower your white blood cells, red blood cells, and platelets, so regular blood tests are very important while you are taking it. It may harm an unborn baby, so both men and women should use reliable birth control while taking it and for a period of time after stopping. Do not breastfeed while on this medication. Tell your doctor about all your other medicines, especially ones that affect your kidneys, because valganciclovir can also affect kidney function.
typical_dosing: For treating CMV retinitis, the usual starting dose is 900 mg (two 450 mg tablets) taken twice a day with food for 21 days, then reduced to 900 mg once daily. For prevention after a transplant, it is typically 900 mg once daily with food. Your doctor will adjust your dose based on how well your kidneys are working.
